MA thesis, University of North Dakota (UND Theses and Dissertations 4470), 145 pp. Open access:https://commons.und.edu/theses/4470(file obtained via archived copy (Internet Archive, 2024) of the UND PDF).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'San Francisco Ozolotepec Zapotec' (phonological sketch), §2.6 'Stress', p. 43 of 145; vowel reduction continues p. 44 with fn. 35; tone §2.4 pp. 37-39; syllable §2.5 pp. 40-43, ex. 17 affixed words); identity statement p. 23; phrase-level primary/secondary stress marks in elicitation frame (25) p. 53
catalog_quote: As stated above, most words are one syllable roots. If a word is multi-syllabic, simply stated, stress falls on the root. Prefixes and clitics never receive primary stress. In compounds or phrases, the stress is usually on the last syllable: gɪl:ˈgiʔd ‘sandal’, ngɪt ˈfrɪt ‘roasted chicken’ (frit ‘fried’ Sp. frito). Vowels in unstressed roots or of suffixes move to a more central vowel space, are reduced phonetically to schwa [ə], and sometimes are deleted, making identification of the vowel phoneme difficult. ... It is often difficult to distinguish the phonemic vowel of clitics, prefixes and affixes as well (e.g. ʃɪ~ʃә- ‘3POSS’, -chə~-cha ‘more’). ... An unstressed vowel will not show phonemic contrast, therefore, it is important to observe vowel correlates preceding fortis consonants in stressed roots.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are mostly monosyllabic roots; in polymorphemic words primary stress falls on the root syllable, never on prefixes or clitics (suffix and prefix vowels reduce to schwa or delete). In compounds and phrases the stress is usually on the last syllable (i.e. the final root).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress is described. Secondary stress is mentioned only at phrase level: in the elicitation frame (p. 53) the target word carries the primary stress of the phrase and a later verb carries secondary stress (marked ˌ).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds/phrases: stress 'usually' on the last syllable (hedged). Unstressed root vowels (e.g. first member of compounds, place names) reduce, so vowel contrasts are neutralised there. The language also has tone: two phonemic tones L and H plus an LH contour, with low functional load (§2.4, p. 37); tones on unstressed affixes are hard to identify (fn. 35, p. 44); SCXZ tones are largely reversed relative to SFOZ.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root vs. affixes/clitics), with a separate remark on compounds and phrases (final). The statement is from the author's 'basic phonological sketch' (she notes on p. 23 that 'there is no published account of the phonological system of SFOZ and SCXZ'); data from the author's field residence in San Francisco Ozolotepec since 2003 and an instrumental study of six male speakers in a carrier frame. Applies to SFOZ; SCXZ differs in tone and some pronunciation but is treated as the same language.
new_statements.identity_note: Leander 2008 describes San Francisco Ozolotepec Zapotec (SFOZ) as its primary variety, with secondary attention to Santa Catarina Xanaguía Zapotec (SCXZ); she states (p. 23) that SFOZ 'is also known as Xanaguía Zapotec', spoken in Santa Catarina Xanaguía, San Francisco Ozolotepec and San José Ozolotepec, all under ISO 639-3 ztg = Glottolog xana1235. The SIL Mexico language page (saved) makes the same identification and warns that the other Ozolotepec towns (San Marcial, San Gregorio) speak a different variety, Ethnologue's 'Ozolotepec Zapotec' [zao] = ozol1235. Note: the earlier access-gap table assigned Heise 2003 to ozol1235; SIL's own page files Heise 2003 under ztg, so that assignment is wrong. Glottolog's alternate name 'Zapoteco de Asunción Tlacolulita' for xana1235 is not used by any source seen here.
